(p-434) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah adh-Dhariyat.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the scatterers, dispersing;﴾ ﴿and the bearers of burdens, carrying;﴾ ﴿and the runners, gliding easily;﴾ ﴿and the distributors of the affair;﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true,﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Recompense is surely going to occur.﴾

The majority of the people of knowledge hold that what is meant by "adh-Dhariyat" (the scatterers) is the winds, and this is the truth, if Allah wills. What supports this is that dhar' (scattering) is a well-known attribute of the winds.

From the same usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So it becomes dry stubble, which the winds scatter﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. The meaning of tadhruhu (scatters) is that it lifts and disperses it. Thus the winds scatter dust, rain and other things. From the same usage is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"And a waterless, desolate watering-place whose traces the winds scatter over its camel-dung, dry pellets."

It is not hidden that the view of those who say that adh-Dhariyat are women is untenable.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿and the bearers of burdens, carrying﴾, the majority of the people of knowledge hold that what is meant by "al-hamilat wiqran" (the bearers of burdens) is the clouds, that is, the heavy clouds that carry a burden, a weight of water.

What supports this view is Allah's explicit description of the clouds as heavy (thiqal), which is the plural of thaqilah, because of the weight of the water-burden they carry, as in His saying: ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 12], where it is the plural of a heavy cloud, and His saying: ﴿until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land﴾ [al-A'raf: 57].

Some have said that what is meant by "al-hamilat wiqran" is the ships that carry the loads of people and their goods. And if someone said that "al-hamilat wiqran" are also the winds, its reading would be clear.

The indication of some verses for this is clear, because Allah, exalted is He, stated that the winds carry the heavy water-laden clouds. Since it is the winds that carry the clouds wherever Allah wills, attributing the carrying of that burden to them is more apparent than attributing it to the clouds, which are themselves carried by the winds. This is in His saying (p-435), exalted is He: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land﴾ [al-A'raf: 57].

So His saying ﴿until, when they carry heavy clouds﴾ means: until, when the winds carry heavy clouds. Here iqlal means carrying, and it is ascribed to the wind. The indication of this for the view that al-hamilat wiqran are the winds is evident, as you see, and it is valid for the verse to encompass all of this.

We have previously stated several times that this is the preferable reading in such cases, and we explained the views of the jurists of legal theory on it, and their discussion of carrying a shared term on both or all of its meanings, at the beginning of Surah an-Nur and elsewhere.

The view that al-hamilat wiqran are the pregnant females carrying fetuses is clearly untenable. As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿and the runners, gliding easily﴾, the majority of the people of knowledge hold that what is meant by "al-jariyat yusra" (the runners gliding easily) is the ships that run upon the sea with ease, that is, a motion accompanied by ease and smoothness.

The more apparent view is that this indefinite verbal noun (yusran) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), as we have previously stated several times: that is, "the runners" while they are made easy, the sea being subjected to them. What supports this view is the frequent application of the description of running to ships, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs are the ships running on the sea﴾ [ash-Shura: 32],

• His saying: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the running ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the ship that runs upon the sea by His command﴾ [al-Hajj: 65],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is He who subjected the sea to you so that the ships may run upon it by His command﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 12],

along with other verses.

It has been said: al-jariyat are the winds, and it has been said other than that.

As for His saying, ﴿and the distributors of the affair﴾: they are the angels whom Allah sends on various affairs and matters. This is why He expressed them as "distributors." What supports this is His saying: ﴿and the governors of the affair﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 5]. Among them are those sent to direct rain and wind, among them those sent to record deeds, among them those sent to seize souls, and among them those sent to destroy nations, as happened to the people of Salih.

The verification is that His saying "amran" (affair) is the direct object of the descriptive term which is "al-muqassimat" (the distributors), and it is a singular noun used to mean the plural.

We have clarified examples of this in the Mighty Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, with the singular being indefinite as here (p-436), and definite and in construct, in the beginning of Surah al-Hajj in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Then We bring you out as a child﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

The matter sworn to by these oaths is His saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true,﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Recompense is surely going to occur.﴾ What necessitates this emphasis is the intensity of the disbelievers' denial of the Resurrection and the recompense.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾, "ma" here is a relative pronoun, the returning pronoun to the relative clause is omitted, and the descriptive term has the sense of a verbal noun. That is: indeed, what you are promised of recompense and reckoning is true, with no falsehood in it.

Some scholars have said: "ma" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), meaning: indeed, the promise of resurrection, recompense and reckoning is true.

Some have said: the form of the active participle in "lasadiq" (true) has the sense of the passive participle, meaning: indeed, the promise or the promised thing is truly fulfilled, not denied. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning "pleasing" (mardiyyah). The truth of what is promised, contained in this noble verse, comes in many verses, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9],

• His saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely coming﴾ [al-An'am: 134],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2],

and verses of this kind are numerous and well known.

Here "ad-din" (the Recompense) means the recompense: that is, indeed the recompense on the Day of Resurrection is certainly going to occur, as He said: ﴿On that Day Allah will pay them their full due in truth﴾ [an-Nur: 25], that is, He will recompense them with justice and fairness, and as His saying: ﴿and that his effort will be seen, then he will be rewarded for it with the fullest reward﴾ [an-Najm: 40–41].

He has also declared Himself far above having created creation without resurrection and recompense, and He made clear that this is the supposition of the disbelievers. He threatened them for that evil supposition with woe from the Fire. He, exalted is He, said, denouncing those who supposed there is no resurrection or recompense, and declaring Himself free from having created them in vain without resurrection and recompense: ﴿Did you then suppose that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115–116].

He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad: 27], where in His saying in this Surah of Sad, "batilan" (in vain) means in vain, without resurrection and recompense.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky with its intricate paths,﴾ ﴿indeed you are in a discordant saying,﴾ ﴿from which is turned away whoever is turned away.﴾

(p-437) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with its intricate paths﴾. Concerning it, the scholars have sayings that are close in meaning and do not contradict one another. Some of the people of knowledge held that al-Hubuk (the intricate paths) is the plural of habikah or hibak, and according to this the meaning is "possessor of paths" (dhat al-hubuk), that is, possessor of the tracks. What appears on the surface of still water or on sand as tracks, when the wind strikes it, is al-hubuk, the plural of habikah or hibak. They said: because of the sky's distance, its tracks, expressed by al-hubuk, are not seen. From this meaning is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Crowned with the roots of stars, woven by a northern wind, in the bright of a hundred tracks (hubuk)."

And the saying of the rajiz (rhymed-verse reciter):

"As if the weavers had covered it, a carpet whose weaving is patterned with hibak."

Among those from whom this saying is transmitted are al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak.

Some of the people of knowledge said: "dhat al-hubuk" means possessor of good, firm creation. Among those who said this are Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah.

This view is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency. Return the gaze; do you see any rifts? Then return the gaze twice; the gaze will return to you humbled while it is fatigued﴾ [al-Mulk: 3–4], along with other verses.

According to this view, al-hubuk is a verbal noun (masdar), because every work whose doer perfected it and made its craft good is called by the Arabs: habakahu habkan, with fatha, according to analogy. Al-hubuk with two dammas has the same meaning.

Some scholars said: dhat al-hubuk means possessor of adornment.

Among those from whom this is narrated are Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan. According to this view, the verse is like His saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. We have already presented the verses clarifying this in Surah Qaf, in discussing His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it?﴾ [Qaf: 6].

Some scholars said: dhat al-hubuk means possessor of strength, and this view is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba': 12].

(p-438) The Arabs call strength of creation habk, and from it is said of a horse of strong build: mahbuk.

From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"He has come carrying me on his nose, a swift horse of strong build, well-knit, with a firm trot."

The verse encompasses all of these, so all the sayings are true. The matter sworn to in this verse is His saying: ﴿indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾, that is, indeed you, O disbelievers, are in a discordant saying concerning the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an, for some of them say it is poetry, some say it is sorcery, some say it is soothsaying, and some say it is the fables of the ancients. As for the view of one who says that "discordant" means that some of them affirm and some deny, it is contrary to the careful verification.

What indicates that the discord is only among the deniers, not the affirmers, is His saying in Qaf: ﴿Rather they denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5]. That is, mixed up; some said: discordant, and the meaning is one.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from which is turned away whoever is turned away﴾. In my view, the most evident of the sayings concerning it, and it should not be departed from in my judgment, is that the particle "'an" (from) in the verse is causal, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and we shall not abandon our gods because of your saying﴾ [Hud: 53], that is, because of your saying and on account of it. The pronoun governed by "'an" refers to the discordant saying. The meaning: "yu'fak" (is turned away), that is, is diverted from belief in Allah and His Messenger. "'anhu" (from it), that is, from that discordant saying, that is, because of it. "man ufik" (whoever is turned away), that is, whoever had wretchedness preordained in eternity, so he was deprived of guidance and was turned away from it, because this discordant saying contradicts itself and refutes itself.

Among the clearest proofs of the falsehood and nullity of a saying is its discord and self-contradiction, as is not hidden. So this discordant saying, by which the disbelievers of Makkah try to bar people from Islam, of which some say the Messenger is a sorcerer, some say a poet, and some say a liar, is evidently null because of its contradiction and because some of it denies the rest. Therefore no one is turned away from Islam because of it except one who is turned away, that is, whom Allah turns away from the truth because of his wretchedness in eternity. Whoever has not had wretchedness and disbelief written for him in Allah's prior knowledge is not turned away from the truth by a saying evidently false and null because of its contradiction.

This meaning is clarified in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship﴾ ﴿are not able to lead astray concerning Him﴾ ﴿except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 161–163].

(p-439) The meaning of this verse is that the religion of the disbelievers, which is associating partners with Allah and worshipping idols, despite their eagerness to bar people from the religion of Islam, "they are not able to lead astray concerning Him" — that is, they cannot lead anyone astray through it, because its corruption and nullity are evident — "except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire," that is, except one for whom Allah has decreed wretchedness and who is among the people of the Fire in His prior knowledge. This is what appears to us as the meaning of this noble verse.

Most of the exegetes hold that the pronoun in His saying ﴿is turned away from it﴾ refers to the Prophet ﷺ or the Qur'an, that is, is diverted from belief in the Prophet or the Qur'an, "whoever is turned away," that is, is diverted from the truth and deprived of guidance, because the truth is so manifest regarding the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ and that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah. This is contrary to the apparent context, as you see.

As for the view of one who said: "is turned away from it" means "whoever is turned away from the discordant false saying," that is, whoever is diverted from falsehood toward truth, its remoteness and weakness are not hidden.

Those who held this view claim that ifk (turning away) is applied to diverting from truth to falsehood and from falsehood to truth. What makes this unlikely is that the Qur'an does not use ifk to mean anything except diverting from good to evil, not the reverse.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾.

It is not hidden from one who has knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of Islamic legal theory) that this noble verse contains the indication well known among the scholars of usul as dalalat al-iima' wa al-tanbih (indication by allusion and alerting), which points to the fact that the cause of attaining these gardens and springs is the taqwa (God-consciousness) of Allah. The legal cause (al-sabab al-shar'i) is the legal ratio (al-'illa al-shar'iyya), according to the most correct view. That taqwa is the cause of entering the gardens, which this noble verse indicates, is made clear in other verses of the Book of Allah, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-conscious﴾ [Maryam: 63]. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in surah al-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish; thus does Allah reward the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 31].

And in the earth are signs for those of certainty (﴿وَفي الأرْضِ آياتٌ لِلْمُوقِنِينَ﴾). And in yourselves; will you not then see? (﴿وَفِي أنْفُسِكم أفَلا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾).

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in the beginning of Surat al-Jathiyah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 22:

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision, and that which you are promised.﴾

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of the provision of people being in the heaven. A group of the people of knowledge held that the meaning is that the origin of all their provisions is the rain, which descends from the heaven. The name "rizq" (provision) is frequently applied to rain in the Qur'an with this meaning, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the heaven﴾ [Ghafir: 13].

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And in the alternation of the night and the day and what Allah sends down from the heaven of provision﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 5].

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in the surah of al-Mu'min (Ghafir).

Allah's sending down of provision from the heaven by sending down rain is among the greatest of His signs that indicate His greatness and that He alone is the one worthy of worship, and among the greatest of His blessings upon His creation in this world. For this reason, the reminder of it is frequent in the Qur'an as a favour upon the creation.

Some of the people of knowledge said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ is that your provisions are predestined and written, and Allah, Majestic and Exalted, manages the affair of the earth from the heaven, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿He manages the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him﴾ [as-Sajdah: 5]. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and that which you are promised﴾: "ma" (that which) is in the place of nominative case, conjoined to His saying "rizqukum" (your provision). The meaning of "that which you are promised," some of the people of knowledge said, is Paradise, because Paradise is above the heavens; so the attribution of its being in the heaven is a correct Arabic usage, for the Arabs apply the word "sama'" (heaven) to everything that is above you, as it has been said:

"Every high thing may be called a heaven, though the excellence lies where the sun and moon are."

When an-Nabighah al-Ja'di recited his well-known poem, he said in it: "Our glory and our loftiness have reached the heaven, and indeed we hope for a manifestation beyond that." He (ﷺ) said to him: "To where, O Abu Layla?" He said: "To Paradise." He said: "Yes, if Allah wills."

Some of the people of knowledge said: that which you are promised, of good and evil, is all predestined in the heaven, as we explained in the second opinion concerning the meaning of "provision" in the verse; and this meaning regarding what they are promised is more suitable to this second opinion concerning the meaning of provision.

Stories have been related which indicate that this is what comes to the mind of the hearer. Among them is what more than one narrator related from Sufyan ath-Thawri, that he said: Wasil al-Ahdab recited this verse, ﴿And in the heaven is your provision, and that which you are promised﴾, (p-441) and said: "Do I not see my provision in the heaven while I seek it on the earth?" So he entered a ruined place and stayed there three days without obtaining anything. Then on the third day, behold, there was a bunch of dates, and he had a brother who was better than him in intention; he entered with him, and they became two bunches, and this continued as their custom until death separated them.

Among them also is what az-Zamakhshari mentioned in the interpretation of this verse. He said: And from al-Asma'i, who said: I came from the congregational mosque of Basra, and a Bedouin appeared upon his she-camel, and said: "From whom are you, man?" I said: "From the Banu Asma'." He said: "From where have you come?" I said: "From a place where the speech of the Most Merciful is recited." He said: "Recite to me." So I recited: ﴿By the scatterers﴾ (adh-Dhariyat). When I reached His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾, he said: "Enough for you." Then he rose to his she-camel, slaughtered it, and distributed it among those who came and went; and he went to his sword and bow, broke them both, and departed. When I performed the pilgrimage with ar-Rashid, I began to circumambulate, and behold, someone was calling out to me in a soft voice. I turned, and behold, it was the Bedouin, emaciated and yellowed. He greeted me and asked me to recite the surah. When I reached the verse, he cried out and said: "We have indeed found what our Lord promised us to be true." Then he said: "Is there anything other than this?" So I recited: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is that you speak﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 23]. He cried out and said: "Glory be to Allah! Who is it that angered the Majestic until He swore? They did not believe Him with His word until they compelled Him to an oath," saying it three times, and his soul departed with it. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace."﴾

As for the rest of the story, we have already explained it in surah al-Hijr, in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ [al-Hijr: 51], and in surah Hud, in the story mentioned there, so repeating it here is unnecessary.

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-400) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah adh-Dhariyat

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾

It is not hidden that there is an apparent contradiction between this adjective and the noun it modifies, because the adjective is in the plural form while the noun it modifies is singular in form.

The answer is that the word ad-dayf (ضيف, "guest") is applied to both the singular and the plural, because its origin is the verbal noun of dāfa (ضاف, "to visit as a guest"), which was transferred from the verbal-noun category to the noun category, as was explained earlier in surah al-Baqarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surat al-Hijr, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains﴾ [al-Hijr: 76], and in other places besides that.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾.

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in Surah Fussilat, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ [Fussilat: 16], and what follows it.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 44:**

(p. 442) His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah Fussilat, in the discussion of His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the punishment of humiliation by the thunderbolt seized them﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the heaven We constructed with strength (bi-aydin), and indeed, We are expanding it.﴾

We have already presented the clarifying verses concerning this in Surah Qaf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We constructed it?﴾ [Qaf: 6], and so on.

Caution:

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿bi-aydin﴾ ("with strength") is not among the attributes of Allah known by this name (yad, "hand"), because His saying bi-aydin is not the plural of yad (hand). Rather, al-ayd means strength (al-quwwa). The morphological pattern (wazn) of His saying here, bi-aydin, is fa'l, whereas the pattern of al-aydi (the plural of yad) is af'ul. Thus the hamza in bi-aydin occupies the place of the first radical (fa'), the ya' occupies the place of the middle radical ('ayn), and the dal occupies the place of the last radical (lam). Had His saying, exalted is He, bi-aydin been the plural of yad, its pattern would have been af'ul, so the hamza would be an added letter, the ya' would occupy the place of the fa', the dal would occupy the place of the 'ayn, and the deleted ya', because the word is defective (manqus), would be the lam.

Al-ayd and al-aad, in the language of the Arabs, mean strength (al-quwwa). A man who is ayd is strong (qawiyy). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87], meaning, We strengthened him with it. Whoever thinks that it is the plural of yad in this verse has erred grossly. The meaning is: "And the heaven We constructed with strength."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus did there not come to those before them any messenger but they said, "A magician or a madman!"﴾ ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾

He, glorified and exalted, mentions in this noble verse that no prophet came to a people ﴿but they said, "A magician or a madman!"﴾, then He said: ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another?﴾, then He turned away from their mutual bequeathing of this with a turning-away of nullification, because they had not been gathered together in one time so that they could bequeath it to one another. So He said: ﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾ That is, the factor that brought them together in unanimously agreeing on denying the messengers and attributing to them sorcery and madness is a unity in transgression (ṭughyān), which is exceeding the limit in disbelief.

This indicates that they agreed only because the hearts of some of them resemble the hearts of others in disbelief and transgression, so their statements to the messengers became similar because of the similarity of their hearts.

And He, exalted, has clarified this meaning in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Thus did those before them say the like of what they say. Their hearts are alike.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 54:

Allah's saying: ﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed.﴾

His negation, glory be to Him, in this noble verse of blame from His Prophet ﷺ indicates that he fulfilled the trust (amanah) and gave sincere counsel (nasihah) to the Ummah.

Allah, exalted is He, has clarified this meaning in other places, such as His saying: ﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favor upon you, and have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and His saying: ﴿Upon you is only the conveyance (of the message), and upon Us is the account﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40]. The verses indicating this meaning are many and well known.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾.

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification (bayan) it contains is that Allah makes a thing serve several wisdoms (hikam), mentioning some of its wisdoms in some places. So we mention the rest of its wisdoms and the verses that indicate them, and we have already presented examples of this.

Among this category is this noble verse, for it contains one of the wisdoms of reminding, namely the hope that the one being reminded will benefit from it, because He, exalted is He, said here "and remind," and He followed it with His saying: ﴿for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾.

Among the wisdoms of this as well is the discharge of the reminder from the obligation of the duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Allah has combined these two wisdoms in His saying: ﴿They said, "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 134].

Among the wisdoms of this as well is standing in for the Messengers in establishing the proof of Allah over His creation on His earth, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the Messengers﴾ [An-Nisa: 165].

(p-444) He has clarified this proof at the end of "Ta-Ha" in His saying: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134].

He alluded to it in Al-Qasas in His saying: ﴿And if not that a disaster should afflict them for what their hands have put forth, they would say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your verses and be among the believers."﴾ [Al-Qasas: 47].

We have already discussed these wisdoms in Surah Al-Ma'idah, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is yourselves; whoever strays will not harm you when you are guided﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 105].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me.﴾

The scholars differed over the meaning of His saying ﴿that they should worship Me﴾. Some of them said: the meaning is, "I did not create them except that the happy among them would worship Me and the wretched among them would disobey Me." Thus the purpose behind creating creation, which is the worship of Allah, is fulfilled through the actions of the happy among them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿So if these disbelieve in it, We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ [al-An'am: 89]. This view was transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan.

The most that follows from this view is that it uses the plural while meaning some of them.

Similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an, and among the clearest of them is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i: ﴿فَإِنْ قَتَلُوكُمْ فَاقْتُلُوهُمْ﴾ ("So if they kill you, then kill them"), taking it from killing (qatl) and not from fighting (qital). We have explained this in several places, and we mentioned that among its Arabic evidence is the saying of the poet:

"The sword of the Banu Abs, when they struck with it, turned away from the hands of Warqa' from the head of Khalid."

So you see him attributing the striking to the Banu Abs, while stating explicitly that the striker whose hand the sword turned away from the head of Khalid, meaning Ibn Ja'far al-Kilabi, was Warqa', meaning Ibn Zuhayr al-Absi.

We have already mentioned in (the commentary on) al-Hujurat that among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 99].

Some scholars said: the meaning of His saying ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ is: "except that they should acknowledge My lordship willingly or unwillingly," because the believer obeys by his own choice, while the disbeliever submits and yields to the decree of his Lord under compulsion. This view was transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Ibn Abbas, and he chose it. It is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. Prostration and worship are both submission and humbling before Allah, may He be exalted and high. The verse indicates that some of them do this willingly and some of them do it unwillingly.

It is reported from Mujahid that he said: ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ means: "except that they should know Me." Some of them cited in support of this view His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], and similar verses, which are numerous in the Qur'an. We have explained its abundance in the Qur'an in Surah Bani Isra'il, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable﴾ [al-Isra': 9].

Some people of knowledge said, and it is also reported from Mujahid, that the meaning of His saying ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ is: "except that I command them to worship Me, so whoever I have granted success among them will worship Me, not other than Him." According to this view, the intention of their worship, indicated by the lam in His saying ﴿that they should worship Me﴾, is a religious, legislative will (irada diniyya shar'iyya), which is the one that necessarily accompanies the command. It is general for all whom the messengers commanded to obey Allah, and not a cosmic, decreed will (irada kawniyya qadariyya). For if it were the latter, all of mankind and the jinn would have worshipped Him, but the reality is otherwise, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship"﴾, up to the end of the surah.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The verification, God willing, regarding the meaning of this noble verse ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ is: "except that I command them to worship Me and test them," that is, I examine them through the obligations, then I recompense them for their deeds: if (their deed is) good, then good, and if (it is) evil, then evil. We only said that this is the verification of the meaning of the verse because it is indicated by clear (muhkamat) verses of the Book of Allah. For He, exalted is He, has stated explicitly in verses of His Book that He created them to test them as to which of them is best in deed, and that He created them to recompense them for their deeds.

He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of Surah Hud: ﴿And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud: 7]. Then He explained the wisdom in that, saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed. But if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is not but obvious magic"﴾ [Hud: 7].

(p-446) He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of Surah al-Mulk: ﴿He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of Surah al-Kahf: ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

So His explicit statement, may He be exalted and high, in these mentioned verses that the wisdom of His creating creation is their being tested as to which of them is best in deed, explains His saying ﴿that they should worship Me﴾. And the best thing by which the Qur'an is explained is the Qur'an itself.

It is known that the outcome of the intended action is not complete except by recompensing the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. Therefore He, exalted is He, stated explicitly that the wisdom of creating them initially and resurrecting them a second time is the recompense of the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. This is in His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of Surah Yunus: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. But those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment for what they used to disbelieve﴾ [Yunus: 4], and His saying in al-Najm: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil for what they have done and reward those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31].

He, exalted is He, has denounced man for his assumption and his thought that he would be left neglected (suda), that is, unattended, not commanded and not forbidden. He explained that He did not move him from stage to stage until He brought him into existence except that He would resurrect him after death, that is, and recompense him for his deeds. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected? Was he not a sperm-drop from semen emitted? … Is not He [who does that] able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36–40].

The proofs for the resurrection indicate the recompense. He, exalted is He, has declared Himself free of this assumption which the disbelievers assumed about Him, that He would not resurrect the creation nor recompense them, denouncing that of them in His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you uselessly and that to Us you would not be returned?﴾ ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth. There is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115–116].

We have already presented the verses that clarify this at the beginning of Surah al-Ahqaf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and that between them except in truth and for a specified term﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 3].

* *

Note (tanbih):

Know that the verses that indicate the wisdom of Allah's creating the heavens and the earth and their inhabitants and what is between them (p-447) may lead one who does not reflect to think that there is a contradiction between them, but the reality is otherwise, because the speech of Allah does not contradict one part of it with another. The clarification of this is that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, mentioned in some verses that the wisdom of His creating the heavens and the earth is to inform His creatures that He is capable of everything and that He encompasses everything in knowledge. This is in His saying, exalted is He, at the end of al-Talaq: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them. The command descends among them that you may know that Allah is competent over all things and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq: 12].

He mentioned in many places in His Book that He created the creation in order to show mankind that He alone is the one worshipped, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. Then He established the proof that He is one God by His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day﴾ up to His saying: ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. When He said: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], He explained that their creation is proof that He alone is the one worshipped, by His saying after it: ﴿who created you and those before you﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 21].

Reasoning that the one worshipped is one because He is the Creator is very abundant in the Qur'an. We have clarified the verses that indicate it at the beginning of Surah al-Furqan, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He created everything and determined it with precise measure﴾ ﴿and they have taken, besides Him, deities that create nothing﴾, the verse [al-Furqan: 2–3]; and in Surah al-Ra'd, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they attributed to Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them? Say, "Allah is the Creator of all things"﴾, the verse [al-Ra'd: 16]; and in other places.

He mentioned in some verses that He created the heavens and the earth in order to test mankind, as in His saying: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His throne was upon the water, that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7].

He mentioned in some verses that He created them to recompense them for their deeds, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾, the verse [Yunus: 4]. He mentioned in this verse of al-Dhariyat that He did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Him. Someone who is not knowledgeable may think that there is a contradiction between these verses, although there is no contradiction among them, because the ruling mentioned in all of them refers to one thing, which is knowing Allah, obeying Him, and knowing His promise and His threat. So His saying: ﴿that you may know that Allah is competent over all things﴾ [al-Talaq: 12] (p-448) and His saying: ﴿Worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21] refer to one thing, which is knowledge of Allah, because whoever knows Allah obeys Him and affirms His oneness.

This knowledge, Allah teaches them it, and He sends messengers to them in accordance with it, so that whoever perishes may perish with clear evidence, and whoever lives may live with clear evidence. So obligation comes after knowledge, and recompense comes after obligation. Thus it became clear that the verses agree, because recompense necessarily requires obligation, which is the trial mentioned in the verses, and obligation necessarily requires knowledge. Therefore some verses indicate that the wisdom of creating the creatures is knowledge of the Creator, some indicate that it is the trial, and some indicate that it is the recompense. All of that is true with no contradiction in it, and some of it is ordered upon some other.

We have explained the meaning of ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), in Surah Hud, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for that He created them﴾ [Hud: 119]. We explained there that the will indicated by the lam in His saying ﴿And for that He created them﴾, that is, for the sake of the difference between wretched and happy, He created them; and in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179] there is a cosmic, decreed will; and that the will indicated by the lam in His saying ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ is a religious, legislative will.

We also explained there the hadiths indicating that Allah created the creation divided into wretched and happy, and that He wrote and decreed that before He created them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is the One who created you; among you is a disbeliever, and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2], and He said: ﴿A party will be in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7].

The upshot is that Allah, through the tongues of His messengers, called all people to believe in Him and to worship Him alone, and commanded them to do so. His command to this effect necessarily entails the religious, legislative will (al-iradah al-diniyyah al-shar'iyyah). Then Allah, exalted is He, guides whomever He wills among them and misguides whomever He wills by His universal, predestining will (al-iradah al-kawniyyah al-qadariyyah), so they arrive at what knowledge has preceded concerning wretchedness and happiness. By this you will know the way of reconciling His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾; and His saying: ﴿And for that He created them﴾; and His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾. We have mentioned that will may be religious and legislative, and it is inseparable from command and approval; and it may be universal and predestining, and it is not inseparable from them both. This is because Allah commands all people to perform the acts willed from them as a religion, while He wills that to occur by way of universal decree and predestination from some of them and not others, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by the permission of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 64]. His saying ﴿except to be obeyed﴾ means: in what he brought from Us, because it is sought and willed from the responsible persons by the law and as religion. His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ indicates that nothing of that occurs except what Allah has willed by universal decree and predestination. And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Each is facilitated for what he was created for." And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a portion (dhanub) like the portion of their companions, so let them not ask Me to hasten.﴾

The original meaning of dhanub (a bucket, a share) in the language of the Arabs is the bucket. It was the custom of the Arabs to divide the water of wells and of the cistern (qalib) by means of the bucket: one would take a bucket's full, and the other would likewise take one. From this they applied the term dhanub, which is the bucket, to a share. A rajiz (rhymed-verse reciter) said, concerning their dividing water by the bucket:

﻿"For us is a dhanub, and for you a dhanub; if you refuse, then for us is the cistern."

It is also related as:

"Indeed, when a drinker shares with us, for him is a dhanub, and for us is a dhanub; but if he refuses, then for us is the cistern."

And from the application of dhanub to a share in general is the saying of Alqama ibn Abada al-Tamimi, though it is said to be Ubayd:

"Among every tribe I have distributed a favour, so Sha's has its due (dhanub) from your generosity."

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"By your life, and the fates are striking, for every family of a father among them there is a dhanub."

So dhanub in the two verses means a share. The meaning of the noble verse is: indeed, for those who wronged by denying the Prophet (ﷺ) there is a dhanub, that is, a share of the punishment of Allah, like the dhanub of their predecessors among the earlier nations, of the punishment they received when they denied their messengers.

This meaning contained in this noble verse has been made clear in many verses of the Book of Allah, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those before them had already said it, but what they earned did not avail them.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they earned befell them, and those who wronged among these people will be struck by the evils of what they earned, and they cannot escape.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 50].

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿so let them not ask Me to hasten﴾, we have previously presented the verses that clarify it in Surah Ar-Ra'd, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though examples have already passed before them﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 6], and in Surah Maryam, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿So do not be hasty concerning them; We are only counting for them a count﴾ [Maryam: 84], and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 51, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from their day which they are promised.﴾

The threat contained in this noble verse, that the disbelievers will face woe (wayl) on the Day of Resurrection because of the punishment of the Fire they will suffer therein, is made clear in many verses,

such as His saying, may He be exalted, in Surah Sad: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, because of the Fire﴾ [Sad 38:27],

and His saying about Ibrahim: ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment﴾ [Ibrahim 14:2],

and His saying in Surah al-Mursalat: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:15].

The verses of this kind are many and well known.

We have already mentioned that the word "wayl" (woe), about which some scholars of knowledge said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) that has no verb derived from its own form, and its meaning is severe destruction. It was also said: it is a valley in Hell from whose heat Hell itself seeks refuge. What justified beginning a sentence with this indefinite noun (nakirah) is that it carries the meaning of supplication (du'a').
